Authors: Qingyang Gao, Cheng Lu, Shou-Jun Huang, Jiu-Sun Zeng
Title: Addressing Covariate Shift in Industrial Soft Sensing Using Conditional Density Ratio-Based Reweighting
Abstract: Data-driven soft sensors in industrial processes often suffer from performance degradation due to covariate shift, where process variable distributions drift over time while the input-output relationship remains unchanged. Existing adaptation methods either struggle to capture complex distribution changes or require additional quality measurements that is unavailable in real time. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a covariate shift adaptation framework for industrial soft sensing using a conditional energy-based model (CEBM). The CEBM models the energies of training and testing data using shared neural network parameters, thereby implicitly defining their probability densities. Since the ratio between two densities depends only on the difference of their energies, the conditional density ratio between the training and testing domains can be obtained directly from the learned energy functions. The estimated density ratio is used to reweight training samples, improving the generalization capability of the soft sensor. To efficiently learn the energy function in CEBM, a Conditional Denoising Score Matching (CDSM) strategy is developed. Furthermore, an online learning mechanism with a replay buffer continuously updates the CEBM using streaming test data and historical samples, enabling real-time density ratio estimation and stable predictive performance under evolving covariate shifts. Experiments on simulated and industrial datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially enhances prediction accuracy.

Authors: Wen-Juan Guo, Wen-Tao Zhang, Shu-Yuan Wang, Rui-Qi Liu
Title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation for Dynamic Distribution Shifts
Source: 2026 6th International Conference on Advanced Algorithms and Neural Networks (AANN)
Abstract: Pre-trained visual models are increasingly deployed in streaming environments where the target distribution changes with weather, illumination, sensor aging, background composition, and time. Existing test-time adaptation (TTA) algorithms usually assume either a fixed target domain or sufficiently large independent test batches; consequently, they can be computationally heavy, slow to converge, and vulnerable to noisy pseudo-supervision under dynamic shifts. This paper presents an efficient online TTA framework for dynamic distribution shifts. The framework contains dynamic confidence screening, branch-level incremental tuning, and temporal distribution smoothness. Only a small set of adaptive branches is updated during inference, while unreliable samples are filtered before optimization and historical batch statistics regularize short-term drift. Experiments on dynamic image classification and object detection streams show average accuracy gains of 4.2%–8.7% over representative TTA baselines and more than 60% lower inference latency than fullparameter continual adaptation. The proposed design provides a practical balance between robustness, stability, and real-time deployment efficiency. Unlike prior TTA designs that treat filtering, lightweight updating, or temporal stabilization separately, the proposed framework couples reliability-dependent sample admission, residual branch-only updating, and statistics-level temporal memory within the same fixed online update budget. Because the classification corruption streams are manually scheduled, the evidence is interpreted as controlled dynamic-benchmark validation rather than a substitute for field deployment.

Authors: C. Padmaja, Rakib Hasan, M. Babu, G. Maheshwari, M. Prabu, Senthilkumar Aandi
Title: ML-Driven Fault Detection in IoT Sensor Nodes using Neuromorphic VLSI Circuits
Source: 2025 IEEE 5th International Conference on ICT in Business Industry & Government (ICTBIG)
Abstract: The growing usage of IoT sensor network in mission critical systems has increased the necessity of having fault detection mechanisms that are reliable and energy efficient. Other traditional ML-based fault detection models, which are precise, are also characterized by high computational cost, higher latency and energy requirements, or excessive power usage, thus not being viable in low-power and large-scale IoT. The given paper introduces a new ML-based fault detection application that is executed by neuromorphic VLSI circuits, making it possible to provide real-time, low-power, and on-node intelligence. The system comprises of the temporal feature extraction, hybrid spike encoding (Rate and TTFS) and a spiking neural network (SNN) design to identify transient, drift and permanent faults directly at the sensor node level. By using a hybrid approach of training, a mix of offline surrogate gradient learning and on-chip STDP adaptation, the real-time tracking of drift and adaptive identification of faults can be done without relying on clouds. The proposed neuromorphic system provides a promising result, as demonstrated by the experimental validation of the 97.6 % detection accuracy, an average latency of 2.8 ms, and $15.8 \mu \mathrm{J}$ energy per decision, which is much better than classical ML models, such as SVM, RF, and CNN. ROC analysis indicates a large AUC of 0.986, and sensitivity tests indicate a strong performance in all types of faults. It also allows early warning alerts using minimal power consumption, and the event-driven spike processing is, therefore, appropriate to long-term (autonomous) IoT deployment. The article offers a scalable, highly efficient (low-powered) platform that offers real-time fault detection, which opens the path to the next-generation neuromorphic-enabled smart IoT infrastructures.

Authors: Qiwei Guo, Zhi-Liang Yu, Jian Zhou
Title: Rate-Dependent Hysteresis Modeling and Hybrid Inverse Compensation Control for Piezoelectric Actuators
Abstract: Highlights What are the main findings? A seventh-order, frequency-dependent rising/falling branch model is selected using validation error and endpoint-stability criteria. A direct inverse feedforward path is integrated with disturbance-observer-based adaptive sliding-mode feedback and verified on a laboratory piezoelectric stack platform. What are the implications of the main findings? The direct inverse model strongly reduces hysteresis nonlinearity, while the feedback loop compensates residual model errors, bounded disturbances, and unmodeled dynamics. The hybrid architecture improves tracking beyond feedforward-only compensation while smooth tanh switching and projection adaptation suppress chattering and parameter drift. Abstract Piezoelectric ceramic actuators are widely used in precision positioning and sensor-integrated micro-motion systems, but their accuracy is limited by asymmetric, rate-dependent hysteresis and by residual disturbances that remain after feedforward linearization. This study develops a self-contained modeling and control framework that combines an explicit rising/falling branch polynomial model, frequency-dependent coefficient maps, direct inverse feedforward compensation, and disturbance-observer-based adaptive sliding-mode feedback. The actuator is represented as a multilayer piezoelectric stack coupled to an equivalent electrical-mechanical-sensing plant. A branch-state logic resolves the multivalued inverse mapping, and a numerical order-sensitivity study shows that the seventh-order model provides the lowest validation RMSE while avoiding the endpoint growth observed at higher orders. Laboratory measurements at 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 Hz, together with attenuated, triangular, random-amplitude, step, and 2 Hz sinusoidal tests, are used for validation. The proposed branch model reduces static maximum relative fitting error from 4.50–6.21% for the classical P-I model to 1.28–2.58%. Direct inverse compensation reduces linearity error from 8.56–13.88% to 0.53–1.024%, and the hybrid controller achieves a 1% settling time of 8.6 ms, a maximum tracking error of 0.0051 micrometers, and an RMSE of 0.0012 micrometers. The results demonstrate an embedded-oriented compromise between model accuracy, online computational simplicity, and robust closed-loop precision.

Authors: Yuan-Zhe Liu, Yang Liu, Cunyu Zhang, Yao Dong, Shuxin Ma, Long-Fei Zhang, Yang Yang
Title: Global-Local Normalization based Model Pool for Online Anomaly Detection in IIoT
Source: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Smart Internet of Things (SmartIoT)
Abstract: Accurate online anomaly detection of multivariate time-series data collected from multiple sensors is crucial for Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) systems. A big challenge of online anomaly detection is how to deal with concept drift, the temporal evolution of intrinsic statistical properties of the data, which induces significant distribution discrepancies between training and testing data. Existing methods failed to adapt to such distribution shifts, leading to low detection accuracy. To address this problem, this paper propose a Global-Local Normalization based Model Pool (GLNMP) framework for accurate online anomaly detection in IIoT. First, a global-local normalization module is designed to simultaneously capture both short-term local anomalies and long-term global pattern changes. Second, we propose an adaptive model pool update module to address both the problem of model adaptation to concept drift and the overfitting problem. Finally, experiments on 10 real-world datasets demonstrate that GLNMP outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

Authors: L. Adams, Timothy Okoliko, Jennifer Okoliko
Title: AgroGuard AI: A Trustworthy Adaptive Architecture for Crop Disease Intelligence under Environmental Non-Stationarity
Source: International Journal of Modern Science and Research Technology
Abstract: Deep learning systems for crop disease recognition are routinely reported at above 95% accuracy on curated benchmarks, yet their field performance degrades sharply and silently once deployed. The cause is not a modelling deficiency in the conventional sense but a violation of the stationarity assumption on which supervised learning rests: the agro-climatic environment that generates the data is itself non-stationary. Humidity regimes shift between seasons, pathogen populations evolve, cultivar mixes change, sensor hardware ages, and the relationship between visual symptom and disease label drifts with them. A model frozen at training time therefore decays monotonically, and — more damagingly for trust — it decays while continuing to report high confidence. This manuscript presents AgroGuard AI, a five-layer reference architecture that treats environmental non-stationarity as a first-class design constraint rather than a deployment nuisance. The architecture couples four mechanisms that are usually studied in isolation. A drift detection subsystem monitors input, representation, and label-conditional distributions using a complementary ensemble of ADWIN, KSWIN, and kernel maximum mean discrepancy tests. A continual learning subsystem combines elastic weight consolidation with sparse episodic replay so that adaptation to a new agro-climatic regime does not erase competence in previously encountered ones. A conformal prediction layer converts raw softmax scores into prediction sets with distribution-free marginal coverage guarantees, and gates low-reliability inputs to human review rather than issuing a confident wrong answer. Finally, a temporal explanation engine reports not only why a prediction was made but why it changed, surfacing the shift in feature attribution that accompanies each adaptation event. We formalise the learning problem, specify each subsystem, derive the adaptation trigger policy, and define a trust metric suite covering calibration error, explanation fidelity, backward transfer, and selective risk. We further specify an edge deployment profile for low-connectivity rural contexts and a privacy-preserving federated aggregation scheme. The manuscript closes with a complete evaluation protocol — datasets, baselines, ablations, and acceptance thresholds — designed to falsify the architecture's central claims. All quantitative values reported herein are design targets and illustrative simulations under explicitly stated generative assumptions; no field trial has been conducted, and this limitation is treated as a defining boundary of the present contribution rather than a caveat.

Authors: Mei Wu, Wen-Chao Weng, Wen Su, Wen-Jie Tang, Wei Zhou
Title: CoMemNet: A Continual Memory Network With Drift-Aware Sampling for Traffic Prediction
Source: IEEE Transactions on Computational Social Systems
Abstract: Traffic sensor networks evolve as sensors are added and traffic distributions change, whereas most forecasting models assume a fixed node set and repeatedly retrain on all available data. We propose CoMemNet, a Continual Memory Network for efficient prediction over evolving traffic sensor networks. CoMemNet uses an Online branch to adapt to the current period and an exponential-moving-average Target branch as a stable feature reference. A Wasserstein-based Drift Sampler compares node-wise Online-Target feature distributions and selects a limited set of drift-sensitive nodes for updating. A lightweight Node-Adaptive Temporal Memory Replay Buffer (TMRB-N) retains compact temporal states without repeatedly traversing all historical training data. The prediction backbone does not consume an adjacency matrix; sensor adjacency is used only to construct data and optionally expand the selected update set to a limited neighborhood. Experiments on three multi-period PeMS datasets include three-seed evaluation, strong static retraining and continual baselines, controlled sampling strategies, continual-learning metrics, robustness tests, and resource accounting. The results show that CoMemNet maintains stable prediction accuracy and efficient adaptation under bounded shared-node selection, achieving a better balance between historical knowledge preservation and current-period prediction performance. Meanwhile, as the evolving network expands, CoMemNet shows clearer accuracy and cumulative training-time advantages over current-period retraining baselines. The code is available at:https://meiwu5.github.io/CoMemNet.

Authors: Dinesh Patil, N. Kubal, Sudhakar Munusamy, Tanuja Joshi, V. Pinnamaraju, Alf J. Isaksson, Fabian Buelow, A. Igave
Title: Evaluation of Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Operation: A Distillation Column Case Study
Abstract: Industrial process autonomy is limited by nonlinear dynamics and the need for operators to handle abnormal events manually. In current practice, economic optimization is managed through a hierarchy of real-time optimization (RTO) and model predictive control (MPC). However, these systems are typically designed for normal operation and rely on human intervention for safety-critical abnormal events. While recent reinforcement learning (RL) studies suggest an alternative to this hierarchy, most use low-fidelity simulators and address control in isolation. This study addresses these gaps by using a high-fidelity CORYS INDISS Plus simulator to implement a dual-agent RL architecture that unifies economic optimization and abnormal event handling within one framework. The first agent manages normal operation during feed-flow disturbances to maximize butadiene and benzene recovery while meeting product quality specifications. This agent acts as a cascade master, adjusting reflux flow, steam flow, and vent flow setpoints. We used the SmoothRecurrentTD3 algorithm, which employs gated recurrent units (GRU) to handle process time delays and smoothing regularizes to reduce valve oscillation. When benchmarked against RTO-MPC baseline on identical cascade setpoints, the RL agent increased combined profit by 9.8% (5256$/h vs 4788$/h). The second agent handles abnormal operations during complete feed loss or lower feed. It uses a safety-oriented reward function to keep reflux and reboiler levels within safe operating bands to prevent pump cavitation and column flooding. This agent was validated over a five-hour test period, with control switched between the economic and safety agents via a feed-flow threshold. RL inference relies on simple function evaluation, which is significantly faster than the iterative optimization required by RTO-MPC. This allows for quicker responses to dynamic disturbances. Field deployment will require further work on agent trust regions, sensor resilience, and adaptation to process drift. This case study provides an empirical benchmark of RL against industrial supervisory control and offers a practical route to reduce operator dependence.

Authors: F. Burgos-Flórez, Juan Guillermo Popayán Hernández, J. Hoyos-Sánchez
Title: Adaptive Multisensor Fusion Using the First Two Moments of the Innovation Under Nonstationary Degradation
Abstract: Adaptive Kalman filters modify the confidence assigned to measurements when sensor quality changes. Many methods monitor innovation energy, although a slowly varying bias can shift its mean without producing large instantaneous innovations. This work proposes a channel-wise adaptation that combines bounded covariance inflation, a test on the mean of the whitened innovation, and a minimum-dwell-time gate. A differential-drive ground vehicle with GNSS, odometry, gyroscope, and magnetometer was simulated. Six conditions, five severity levels, and forty paired repetitions per cell were studied. A nominal EKF, a mistuned EKF, covariance matching, Sage-Husa, robust Huber weighting, and the proposed method were compared. Position RMSE predicted tracking RMSE with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.994, but the association fell to 0.491 for recovery time. Second-moment methods responded to variable noise and outliers but did not correct drifting bias. The first-moment test enabled action against this shift, although exclusion exhibited a bimodal distribution and improved 28 of 40 repetitions. Minimum dwell time reduced nominal switching. At maximum severity, test-triggered compensation improved upon the nominal EKF in all 40 repetitions, with a median improvement of 67.0% and a nominal cost of 32.2%. No action simultaneously dominated nominal performance, median bias performance, and dispersion. Adaptation should distinguish variance and mean changes and should be evaluated using average, transient, and nominal-cost metrics.

Authors: Jagan Murugesan, P. Vijitha, L. J. Vinita, A. Parvathy, P. N. Jeipratha
Title: Robust vision transformer adaptation for UAV imagery
Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform well on clean aerial imagery but degrade sharply when deployed in post-earthquake UAV operations, where motion blur, dust haze, illumination variation, and sensor noise combine to produce what we term post-earthquake visual drift, a structured distributional shift that can render an otherwise capable model dangerously unreliable in the field. Retraining or conventional domain adaptation is not a realistic option under the latency, compute, and annotation constraints of active disaster response. This work presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation of lightweight label-free test-time adaptation (TTA) methods for improving the robustness of ViTs under such deployment conditions, systematically comparing consistency-based self-supervision (MEMO) and entropy minimization (TENT) across datasets with varying classification complexity. Consistent with existing lightweight TTA approaches, only the LayerNorm affine parameters are adapted during inference, while the backbone and attention weights remain frozen. On the UAV-TEBDE post-earthquake dataset, accuracy rises from 73.47% under severe drift (severity 0.3) to 89.18% using MEMO, corresponding to a recovery of 15.71 percentage points over the drifted baseline, without using any ground-truth labels or performing any retraining. On UAV-TEBDE, MEMO also achieved higher recovery than the SAR baseline evaluated in this study. Additional evaluation on AID (30-class aerial scene classification) and UC Merced (21-class land-use classification) shows consistent drift-induced degradation and adaptation-driven recovery across datasets of varying complexity. The cross-dataset evaluation further reveals that the relative effectiveness of lightweight TTA methods depends on the classification-space dimensionality. TENT-based entropy minimization outperforms consistency-based MEMO when the class count is large, while MEMO is the stronger choice in low-class settings. This interaction between method design and classification-space dimensionality has direct consequences for choosing TTA strategies in operational disaster assessment pipelines. Feature-space PCA analysis confirms that LayerNorm-only updates geometrically recalibrate internal representations, rather than simply correcting the model's output logits.

Authors: Chuan-Hao Liu, Cheng-Liang Zhang, Yan-Qiu Huang, Fu-Biao Ti, Guang-Hui Meng, Qi Wang
Title: A Real-Time Health Management Method for Rolling Mills Based on RPC-Former
Abstract: In an aluminum hot rolling process, where support bearings undergo sudden load changes and rapid speed variations several times per minute, these variations lead to significant baseline shifts in the vibration and temperature signals. However, true fault cases only appear occasionally after several months. Therefore, the supervised learning methods usually presented in laboratory experiments do not have much practical application value. In this paper, we propose the Reconstruction-Prediction Coupling Transformer (RPC-Former), an unsupervised model which is trained directly on the normal operating data. A single backbone is used to reconstruct the current time windows and forecast the short-term future states. The continuous sensor records are normalized using Reversible Instance Normalization (RevIN) and divided into temporal segments to deal with the baseline drift problem. A dynamic Channel and Spatial Adaptation (CASA) coordinate attention mechanism is employed to extract cross-channel and time-block features. The reconstruction and prediction errors constitute a comprehensive health index for multi-level warnings. The model was tested on the hot rolling line data and achieved a joint root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.06247 in the ablation tests and detected a reducer bearing fault 4.8 days earlier than the manual detection.

Authors: Xuhang Wu, Zhuo-Xuan Liang, Wei Li, Xiao Jia, Abdelsalam Helal
Title: PlugSI: Plug-and-Play Test-Time Graph Adaptation for Spatial Interpolation
Source: International Conference on Database Systems for Advanced Applications
Abstract: With the rapid advancement of IoT and edge computing, sensor networks have become indispensable, driving the need for large-scale sensor deployment. However, the high deployment cost hinders their scalability. To tackle the issues, Spatial Interpolation (SI) introduces virtual sensors to infer readings from observed sensors, leveraging graph structure. However, current graph-based SI methods rely on pre-trained models, lack adaptation to larger and unseen graphs at test-time, and overlook test data utilization. To address these issues, we propose PlugSI, a plug-and-play framework that refines test-time graph through two key innovations. First, we design an Unknown Topology Adapter (UTA) that adapts to the new graph structure of each small-batch at test-time, enhancing the generalization of SI pre-trained models. Second, we introduce a Temporal Balance Adapter (TBA) that maintains a stable historical consensus to guide UTA adaptation and prevent drifting caused by noise in the current batch. Empirically, extensive experiments demonstrate PlugSI can be seamlessly integrated into existing graph-based SI methods and provide significant improvement (e.g., a 10.81% reduction in MAE).

Authors: Ting-Han Shi, Kea-Tiong Tang, Shih-Wen Chiu, Pang-Chun Liu
Title: Meta-Learning on Electronic-Nose Time Series for Long-Term Drift Compensation in Metal Oxide Gas Sensor Arrays
Source: 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Olfaction and Electronic Nose (ISOEN)
Abstract: Long-term drift in metal oxide gas sensor arrays remains a major obstacle for reliable electronic-nose deployment. Recent work has shown that meta-learning can mitigate drift on legacy feature-engineered datasets, but the behavior of modelagnostic meta-learning (MAML) on raw time-series responses from modern electronic noses is still unclear. In this work we present an initial empirical study of MAML on the “Long-term drift behavior in metal oxide gas sensor arrays” one-year dataset, which provides 700 recordings from a 62-sensor commercial electronic nose with both raw signals and pre-extracted features. We first establish a supervised 1D residual network baseline trained on early days and tested on later days, confirming strong accuracy degradation due to drift. We then define day-wise and batched-day meta-learning tasks and apply MAML directly to the raw multi-channel sensor responses under few-shot adaptation. Our results show that naïvely applying MAML on this dataset does not automatically outperform a well-tuned supervised baseline; instead, performance is sensitive to task construction and optimization details. We situate these findings with respect to prior feature-based meta-learning work and discuss implications for future electronic-nose algorithms on long-term drift datasets.

Authors: Ali Shahsavandi, Parimehr Morassafar, Kamyar Taeb, A. Beheshti
Title: SPEC-TTA: A Lightweight Spectral Adaptation Framework for Self-Correcting Consumer Edge AI
Abstract: Deep learning models deployed on consumer edge devices for time-series forecasting degrade due to distribution shift caused by changing user behaviors, environmental fluctuations, and sensor degradation. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables on-device self-correction, but existing methods require backpropagation through large backbone networks: full backbone fine-tuning exceeds the typical static random-access memory (SRAM) budget of the host microcontroller (MCU), even embedded-friendly variants retain 3–<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$4\!\times \!$ </tex-math></inline-formula> the activation memory of the proposed approach, and standard MCU neural-network (NN) toolchains provide no backward kernels. We introduce SPEC-TTA, a parameter-efficient spectral adaptation framework that models distribution drift as amplitude scaling, phase shifts, and temporal misalignment in the frequency domain. SPEC-TTA wraps a frozen backbone with three lightweight modules: 1) sparse spectral adapter applying learnable gains to the top-<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$K$ </tex-math></inline-formula> Fourier bins; 2) time-shift head leveraging the Fourier Shift Theorem with a single delay parameter <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\tau _{c}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> per channel; and 3) affine trend head for bias correction. Drift-triggered proximal updates conserve energy by adapting only upon detecting a distribution shift. Across 8 datasets and 4 backbones (96 dataset–backbone–horizon configurations), SPEC-TTA is the selected single winner in 34 cases, a plurality among seven TTA methods, and is best-or-tied in 41 cases, with gains concentrated on datasets exhibiting both strong spectral concentration and non-trivial residual structure (ETT family, Weather), matched-but-not-improved performance on the weakly-periodic Exchange-Rate stress test, and a near-saturation case on Electricity suggesting that high spectral concentration alone is insufficient when the frozen backbone already captures the dominant mode. The full adaptation pipeline fits within 84.3 KB SRAM and adds 1.1% per-window latency overhead on triggered full-adaptation windows (0.4% on non-trigger windows; <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\approx 0.7$ </tex-math></inline-formula>% steady-state at the default 41% trigger rate) under Cortex-M7 (Renode) emulation, with 469 trainable parameters for the profiled 7-channel PatchTST configuration (general count: <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$C(2K{+}3)$ </tex-math></inline-formula> for <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$C$ </tex-math></inline-formula> channels and <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$K$ </tex-math></inline-formula> selected Fourier bins).

Authors: P. Shelar
Title: Regime-Aware Evidence Fusion for Calibrated Forecasting of Non-Stationary Time Series
Source: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
Abstract: Non-stationary forecasting is not the same as forecasting in average terms; forecasting performance depends on the ability to forecast regime changes rather than the ability to fit perfectly in average cases. Regime shifts, calendar effects, policy interventions, and unreliable instrumentation constantly disrupt energy grids, transportation networks, and sensor-intensive urban systems, while even the most commonly-used energy- and transport-related learning-based forecasters typically assume that such systems are near-stationary or incorporate a fragile change-point detector as a pre-processing module. We choose a rather alternative path: discover the regime, gain insight into context, tailor or rate uncertainty, and continuously adapt. All these steps are learnable steps in the pipeline, from the beginning, not added on in a later phase. The five phases create this structure, which functions as follows. Under a causal-invariance constraint, a causal regime tokeniser (CaRT) is able to learn causal-invariance changes in tokens and small context pieces. A Wavelet–State-Space Dual-Path Predictor (WSDP) subsequently is used to predict in the short, medium and long-range combining regime conditioned wavelet decomposition with a neural path space model. A module called 'evidence-weighted fusion' (EviFuse) combines the two forecasts with a (reliability-based) 'weight' determined by the residual. A counterfactual, cross-regime validation suite (CF-XValid) is introduced to stress-test the entire pipeline system, but not just rolling splits to generate new counterfactual scenarios. Last, a drift-aware continual-learning module (DriftShield-ACL) is utilized to maintain honest uncertainty estimates in production with light-weight adapter updates and conformal online updates. The framework reduces mean absolute error by 12–18% compared with the best of three current frameworks on four multivariate, highly non-stationary benchmarks, and lowers the RMSE across long-horizon (96-step) testing by 10–15% compared to the best of three contemporary ones in the targeted 96-step horizon. Its error rate drops more so when up to 20% of exogenous inputs are unavailable, as compared to any baseline, and its 90% prediction intervals remain around nominal (88–89%) as compared to many baselines, which are one or more points below. With compound stress (fast changing levels, beds of high demand, loss of sensors), the worst-case error decreases by approximately 20% compared to the best baseline. Overall, the findings indicate that the regime awareness method, the multi-scale modelling approach, the evidence-based fusion approach and the calibrated adaptation method are more effective as an integrated design of a "combined system" rather than simply as a collection of fixes and more effective when tested within robustness and deployment trust, not only average accuracy.
